routes.label: Locate six roots and prove a degree-six upper bound
Find six roots and bound their number

question: How many values of \(\theta\) in the interval \(0\lt\theta\le 2\pi\) satisfy the following equation? \[1-3\sin\theta+5\cos 3\theta=0\]
solution:
At successive multiples of \(\pi/3\), the term \(5\cos3\theta\) alternates between \(5\) and \(-5\). Its size guarantees alternating signs, which will locate six solutions.

Define
\[
F(\theta)=1-3\sin\theta+5\cos3\theta.
\]
For \(k=0,1,\ldots,6\), we have \(\cos(3k\pi/3)=(-1)^k\). Since \(-1\le\sin\theta\le1\),
\[
F(k\pi/3)\ge3>0\quad\text{when }k\text{ is even},
\]
and
\[
F(k\pi/3)\le-1<0\quad\text{when }k\text{ is odd}.
\]
Sine and cosine are continuous, so \(F\) has at least one zero in each of the six disjoint intervals
\[
\left(\frac{k\pi}{3},\frac{(k+1)\pi}{3}\right),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,5.
\]
Thus there are at least six solutions. We must still rule out additional ones.

The angle-addition and double-angle formulas give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\cos3\theta
&=\cos2\theta\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\sin\theta\\
&=(1-2\sin^2\theta)\cos\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\\
&=\cos\theta(1-4\sin^2\theta).
\end{aligned}
\]
At any solution, let \(s=\sin\theta\). Then
\[
5\cos\theta(1-4s^2)=3s-1.
\]
Squaring and using \(\cos^2\theta=1-s^2\) shows that \(s\) must satisfy
\[
25(1-s^2)(1-4s^2)^2-(3s-1)^2=0.
\]
The left side is a polynomial of degree \(6\), with leading coefficient \(-400\), so it has at most six distinct roots. This follows from the factor theorem: each distinct root supplies a different linear factor.

Moreover, one value of \(s\) cannot give two solutions of the original equation. The values \(s=\pm\tfrac12\) are impossible, because they make \(1-4s^2=0\) while \(3s-1\ne0\). For every other \(s\), the original equation fixes
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{3s-1}{5(1-4s^2)}.
\]
The sine and cosine together determine at most one angle in \(0<\theta\le2\pi\). Hence there are at most six solutions.

Combining the two bounds gives exactly \(\boxed{6}\) solutions, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
